item.title: 6 of the Best Soave Wines From Italy’s Veneto
item.description: Soave, the large and once easily dismissed appellation in Italy’s northeast Veneto region, produces some of Italy’s most exciting white wines. Actually, it always has, but was overshadowed by industrial-scale winemaking that took root in the 1970s and ’80s as the Soave zone was greatly expanded. Soave became synonymous with cheap, insipid, industrial wines — the white-wine companion to the red Valpolicella, also from the Veneto. item.title: You’ve Heard of West Coast IPAs, but What Is a West Coast Pilsner?
item.description: The India pale ale (IPA) is easily the world’s most popular beer style, skyrocketing to the top of the craft beer canon in the late 20th century. By the mid-2010s, the style was virtually inescapable in taprooms and bottle shops, with offerings dominated by the New England (or hazy) IPA subcategory. item.title: We Asked 17 Wine Pros: Which European Wine Regions Offer the Best Value?
item.description: Certain historic “Old World” wines like Burdungy, Barolo, or Bordeaux often get a reputation as overly expensive. In some cases, the high price tag is justified. Many European winemakers with decades of experience are producing excellent wines using coveted, small plots of land that have been cultivated for centuries. item.title: 6 Underrated White Wines From Historically Red-centric Regions
item.description: When you picture a glass of wine, you’re likely to picture a glass of red. When you think of winemaking regions, Bordeaux and Burgundy — both predominantly known for their red wine — come to mind. And when drinkers are surveyed on their preferences, red comes out on top. The instinctual default to red wines makes sense: Many of the most prestigious estates are most known for their reds. item.title: A Timeline of the Bar Industry’s Darling Liqueurs
item.description: When thinking about cocktails, base spirits tend to be the first element that comes to mind. It makes sense — given their high proof, liquors are the primary booze source for most cocktails, both classic and modern. These liquors are undeniably important, but in most instances, they are not the primary flavor driver of the drinks they’re used to create.
